project_name: Pinecrest Mill kraft lignin cake (fictional): dashboard assessment
disclaimers: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.
BioValue AI gives indicative decision support. It does not guarantee profitability, does not verify customer demand, and does not constitute engineering approval.

Gross margin, profitability, NPV, and IRR are not calculated. They need capital costs, fixed costs, a discount rate, a time horizon, and agreed definitions, none of which are available yet. Gross contribution excludes capital costs, fixed costs, and the value of the feedstock in its current use.
Scores use a 1-5 scale. A criterion that was not assessed lowers data completeness; it is never counted as a low score.

constraints: The stream leaves the mill as wet cake and no lignin dryer is available, so buyers requiring dry powder would need drying before use.
The lignin is currently fired in the mill's boilers as internal fuel, so commercial diversion would affect the existing fuel route.
Solvent or membrane fractionation is not available, limiting uses that require molecular fractionation.
Chemical modification equipment is not available, limiting modified-lignin product pathways.
Moisture is uncertain, affecting dry-mass availability and the quantity that must be shipped.
Molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium content are missing, so pathways with requirements for these properties cannot yet be screened reliably.
data_quality_notes: This is fictional demo data, not measured data from a real mill; it must be replaced with mill laboratory data and production records before decisions are made.
The record's lignin-content analytical method is unclear and stated for illustration only.
Moisture is identified as uncertain and should be verified through operating-period sampling.
The recorded dry-matter balance and listed composition-total checks passed validation.
The missing molecular-weight, phenolic-hydroxyl, and sodium fields each have corresponding data-gap entries.
agent.summary: Validated fictional profile for a washed softwood kraft lignin filter cake: the recorded conversion and dry-matter balance pass, but commercial assessment remains provisional because the data are illustrative and several pathway-relevant properties are missing.

data_gaps.impact: Every figure in this profile is invented for demonstration. Results based on it say nothing about a real mill.
data_gaps.next_step: Replace the profile with the mill's own lab data and production records.

data_gaps.impact: Molecular weight can't be compared with any pathway requirement until it is measured.
data_gaps.next_step: Commission a lab analysis of molecular weight distribution, and record the method used.

data_gaps.impact: Phenolic hydroxyl content can't be compared with any pathway requirement until it is measured.
data_gaps.next_step: Commission a lab analysis of hydroxyl group content, and record the method used.

data_gaps.impact: The make-up of the ash is unknown, so ash-related requirements can only be checked against total ash.
data_gaps.next_step: Request an inorganic element analysis of the ash.

data_gaps.impact: Reported lignin content depends on what the analysis counts. The method here is stated for illustration only.
data_gaps.next_step: Confirm the analytical method with the lab and use the same one when comparing with buyers' specifications.

data_gaps.impact: Moisture sets the dry tonnage (dry matter = wet quantity x (1 - moisture)) and the mass that has to be shipped.

checks.disclaimer: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.

current_use.description: Fictional: the precipitated lignin is fired in the mill's own boilers in place of purchased fuel. The unit was built to relieve the recovery boiler, not to sell lignin.

geographic_market.logistics: Fictional: rail siding at the mill; the nearest deep-water port is assumed to be about 150 km away.

supported_claims.EV-PF-01#1: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#4: Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#1: UPM states that its lignin can replace up to 80% of the phenol in lignin-phenol-formaldehyde (LPF) resin.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#2: UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
supported_claims.EV-PF-03#3: With phenol at around 1,000 USD per tonne, substituting part of the phenol in PF resins with lignin is estimated to add about 800 USD per marginal tonne of pulp (not per tonne of lignin); the additional operating costs are not known.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#2: Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#R1: Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#3: UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
supported_claims.EV-PF-04#2: With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#3: A 2018 report cited by the IEA estimates the technology readiness level (TRL) for producing biobased phenolic resins at 8.

applications.statement: The evidence supports kraft lignin as a partial phenol replacement in phenol-formaldehyde resins for plywood and other wood-based panels.
Lignin-phenol-formaldehyde resin has been reported for veneer plywood at up to 80% phenol replacement in a vendor account.

target_customers.statement: The relevant customer types are plywood producers and manufacturers of other wood-based panels that use PF adhesives.

competing_materials.statement: The incumbent material is phenol used in phenol-formaldehyde resins.

qualification_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin requires activation or depolymerization before use in PF resins.
One industrial LPF resin account reports compliance with EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood and reports formaldehyde emissions using EN 717-2.
A laboratory study evaluated resin viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde against a Chinese wood-adhesive standard when depolymerized lignin supplied 50% of the phenolic component.

limitations: The strongest commercial-performance evidence is vendor technical literature, and its performance and cost claims lack a cited test report.
The reported TRL 8 applies to biobased phenolic resins generally, not specifically to kraft lignin; the reported TRL 9 is from a techno-economic comparison.
Several results are laboratory studies or review summaries rather than demonstrations using Pinecrest lignin.
missing_information: No current lignin price, delivered price, demand volume, named buyer, contract terms, or regional market split is provided.

The evidence does not establish whether Pinecrest's wet cake can meet the required resin input condition; the feedstock profile states that no dryer or chemical-modification equipment is available (feedstock:constraints[0]; feedstock:constraints[3]).
Pinecrest lignin molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium content are missing, limiting reliable screening of property-dependent resin routes (feedstock:missing_properties).

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents industrially proven LPF resin and wood-panel performance, but it does not document commercial sales by a lignin producer or several established buyers.

supported_claims.EV-PU-01#1: Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
supported_claims.EV-PU-02#1: Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#1: Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#3: Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#1: The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#2: In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#R1: Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#R1: Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
supported_claims.EV-PU-05#1: Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

applications.statement: The evidence supports kraft lignin as a partial replacement for petroleum-based polyols in rigid polyurethane/polyisocyanurate foam.

The evidence also supports unmodified lignin at 20 wt% petroleum-polyol replacement in laboratory flexible polyurethane foam, with kraft lignin suggested for denser, stiffer or heavy-duty foam applications.
The broader documented polyurethane pathway includes foams, panels, coatings, and rubber replacement.

target_customers.statement: Relevant customer types include rigid insulation-foam manufacturers and flexible-foam manufacturers.
Automotive flexible-foam manufacturers or suppliers are a potential customer type, although the evidence indicates kraft lignin was less suitable for automotive flexible foam than organosolv lignin.

competing_materials.statement: The incumbent material is petroleum-based polyol.

qualification_requirements.statement: The cited acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production is total hydroxyl value above 200 mg KOH/g, or 3.56 mmol/g total hydroxyl groups.
Rigid PUR/PIR foam performance was assessed against ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Kraft lignin generally needs significant treatment such as oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction to reach target polyurethane properties.

limitations: Most evidence is from laboratory foam studies, and the reported kraft-lignin results vary by lignin source and formulation.
The TRL 6 rating applies to a broad polyurethane row rather than specifically to kraft-lignin foam.
A review identifies low consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs as continuing commercialization limitations; its full text was unavailable.
missing_information: No current lignin or polyol price, market volume, named buyer, qualification contract, or regional demand estimate is provided.

Pinecrest's total hydroxyl value is not supplied, and its chemical-modification equipment is unavailable, creating a direct screening gap for the cited polyurethane routes (feedstock:missing_properties; feedstock:constraints[3]).
The wet-cake condition and lack of a dryer are not reconciled with the processing requirements of prospective polyurethane customers (feedstock:constraints[0]).

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence shows research-scale foam trials and a broad TRL assessment, but it does not document commercial sales, established buyers, or a development pilot specifically for Pinecrest-type kraft lignin.

supported_claims.EV-CM-01#1: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#1: DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#4: Mechanical properties of lignin-based carbon fibers were about 50% of the target in this work.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#1: A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#2: Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#1: Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#1: The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#1: Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#2: The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R1: Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R2: Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R3: Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R4: Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R5: Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R1: Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R2: Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#R1: Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#2: Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.

applications.statement: The evidence supports lignin as a precursor for carbon fiber, although the cited carbon-fiber studies identify demanding purification and spinning challenges.
The evidence supports kraft lignin-derived hard carbon for sodium-ion battery anodes.
The evidence supports lignin conversion to activated carbon, including use of precursor lignin that is too impure for other carbon-material applications.

target_customers.statement: Relevant customer types include carbon-fiber producers and industrial users seeking carbon fiber for automotive applications.
Relevant customer types include sodium-ion battery and battery-anode manufacturers.
Battery manufacturers and carmakers are named as qualification counterparts for lignin-based anode material.
Activated-carbon producers are an implied customer type because the evidence describes lignin conversion into activated carbon.

competing_materials.statement: The incumbent carbon-fiber precursor is PAN-based fiber.
For sodium-ion battery hard carbon, anthracite and cellulose are listed as comparison feedstocks, with anthracite representing a fossil precursor option.
Conventional activated carbon is the competing material for the activated-carbon application.

qualification_requirements.statement: The cited ORNL carbon-fiber precursor specification requires lignin content greater than 99%, ash below 0.1% by weight, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm, and removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
The cited kraft-lignin carbon-fiber work required purification, and softwood lignin requires a plasticizing agent for melt spinning.
Lignin-based anode material may require qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers; one company states that this qualification can take 3 years.
Activated carbon has no strict precursor-quality limitation, although lower ash improves yield.

limitations: The carbon-fiber precursor specifications are demanding, are cited secondhand, and were not met for volatiles by any lignin sample in the cited study.
The GreenLight evidence is a project summary with modelled costs; its TRL 5 applies to precursor-fiber production rather than the complete lignin-to-carbon-fiber chain.
The hard-carbon evidence is a review focused on sodium-ion batteries, while the battery-company evidence concerns lithium-ion batteries and provides no lignin quality specification.
The activated-carbon evidence is laboratory work using zinc chloride activation.
missing_information: No current Pinecrest-specific price, product volume, named purchase order, buyer list, or regional demand estimate is provided.
No Pinecrest ash, lignin purity, volatiles, carbohydrate, particulate, or metal measurements are available, so carbon-fiber precursor compliance cannot be screened (feedstock:missing_properties).
The feedstock profile states that solvent or membrane fractionation is unavailable, while fractionation is relevant to some carbon-material processing routes (feedstock:constraints[2]).
The wet-cake condition and lack of a dryer may require additional preparation before downstream carbon processing, but the evidence does not quantify that requirement (feedstock:constraints[0]).

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents an industrially relevant precursor-fiber development project and a pilot anode-material line with stated qualification partnerships, but it does not establish several producers selling to established buyers.

processing_requirements.statement: The wet cake would need drying before any buyer requiring dry powder can use it.
Kraft lignin requires activation or depolymerization before use in phenol-formaldehyde resins.
The resin route would require qualification for plywood or other wood-panel applications, including bonding and formaldehyde-emissions performance.

technical_maturity.statement: A LignoBoost-plus-resin phenol-substitution route is reported at TRL 9, mapping to the highest technical-readiness score.

adoption_barriers.statement: Pinecrest lacks chemical-modification equipment, while the pathway requires activation or depolymerization.
Pinecrest lacks a lignin dryer, and moisture is uncertain, so product conditioning and shipment specifications remain unresolved.
Molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium content are missing, limiting property-dependent resin screening.
Commercial diversion would affect the mill's current boiler-fuel route, and a buyer, contract, demand volume, and delivered-price basis have not been identified.

validation_steps.action: Build a measured process and mass balance for drying, polyurethane modification, resin preparation, and representative carbon-material preparation, including product yield and energy demand.

validation_steps.action: Obtain sourced regional price and demand data, named-buyer specifications, qualification protocols, and written expressions of interest or pilot commitments for each pathway.

validation_steps.action: Prepare a project-level economic model using the measured yield, price, variable costs, capital, logistics, drying, qualification, and modification costs, and subtract the value of displaced boiler fuel.
validation_steps.reason: Polyurethane economics currently rely on indicative analyst assumptions, while phenolic-resin and carbon-material economics are unassessed.

ranking_changers: A measured feedstock-compatibility result for phenolic resins could unlock its currently insufficient-data pathway; its high technical-readiness score and attractiveness range make it the most likely candidate to challenge the current ranking.

Replacing the polyurethane analyst-assumed economics with sourced price, measured yield, conversion cost, capital, drying, modification, and boiler-fuel opportunity-cost data could substantially lower or confirm its rank-1 position.

Product-specific carbon-material compatibility and economics—especially for an activated-carbon or battery-material route rather than the checked carbon-fiber route—could remove the current compatibility penalty and change the relative order.
A real customer qualification or purchase commitment, or failure to qualify, could change the market-evidence and commercialization-feasibility scores across the pathways.
caveats: The Pinecrest feedstock and dashboard case are fictional, so the result is a screening assessment rather than a bankable investment decision.
The ranking is the deterministic engine's ranking. Phenolic resins are not ranked because only 0.55 of weighted criteria were assessed; an unassessed criterion is missing evidence, not a poor score.

Polyurethane indicative economics score 5 is based on an analyst-assumed gross contribution of 1,850.00 USD per tonne of usable dry feedstock and excludes capital costs, fixed costs, and the current fuel-route value.
No product output, revenue, variable cost, gross contribution, or contribution per tonne was calculated for phenolic resins or carbon materials; carbon-material economics therefore remain unassessed.

The technical-readiness evidence describes documented pathway configurations and does not prove that Pinecrest's wet cake, unavailable dryer, unavailable chemical-modification equipment, or current boiler-fuel tradeoff can meet them.
report.summary: The deterministic ranking places polyurethanes first, carbon materials second, and phenolic resins as insufficient data. Polyurethanes lead because of the assessed economics score of 5, despite unresolved feedstock compatibility and major processing and qualification needs. Carbon materials have stronger market evidence but a checked carbon-fiber compatibility score of 1 and no economics assessment. Phenolic resins appear most promising on technical maturity and unadjusted attractiveness, but require feedstock and economics validation before they can be ranked.

documented_facts.statement: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
UPM states that its lignin can replace up to 80% of the phenol in lignin-phenol-formaldehyde (LPF) resin.
UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.

With phenol at around 1,000 USD per tonne, substituting part of the phenol in PF resins with lignin is estimated to add about 800 USD per marginal tonne of pulp (not per tonne of lignin); the additional operating costs are not known.
Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
A 2018 report cited by the IEA estimates the technology readiness level (TRL) for producing biobased phenolic resins at 8.
Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.

Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
Mechanical properties of lignin-based carbon fibers were about 50% of the target in this work.
A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.

The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
A techno-economic comparison lists LignoBoost extraction combined with phenol substitution in resins ('LB+Resin') at TRL 9.
